newsitem.title: FRANCE: Hard right and left ahead in French by-election.
newsitem.headline: Hard right and left ahead in French by-election.

text.p: Communist and extreme rightist candidates humiliated mainstream parties by topping the polls on Sunday in the first round of a by-election to replace bankrupt tycoon Bernard Tapie in France's parliament.

The by-election in this depressed working-class town near Marseille in southern France was widely regarded as a test of the weakness of the mainstream Left and Right 18 months before the 1998 general election.

Officials said Gardanne's Communist mayor Roger Mei won 37 percent of the vote ahead of Damien Barriler of Jean-Marie Le Pen's anti-immigrant National Front party who got 26 percent of votes among the constituency's 100,000 voters.
The two, who will face each other in the run-off next Sunday, saw their scores shoot up from the 1993 general election with Mei gaining 18 percent and Barriler gaining seven percent.

Both Communists and extreme rightists feed on fears of unemployment -- the coal mine that is Gardanne's biggest employer with 4,000 jobs is due to close in 2005 -- and immigration, especially after recent incidents of racial violence in neighbouring Marseille.
The Communist-National Front run-off is a major embarrassment for France's mainstream politicians, suggesting that they have no answer to voters' main concerns.

Herve Fabre-Aubrespy, candidate of the ruling centre-right majority got 15 percent of the vote and the Gaullist Rally for the Republic party, which backed him together with the Union for French Democracy, said it would make no recommendations to its followers for next Sunday's vote.
Fabre-Aubrespy lost 12 percentage points compared to 1993.

Bernard Kouchner, a national political celebrity, former health and humanitarian action minister who was "parachuted" into the race as Radical-Socialist candidate with the backing of the mainstream opposition Socialist Party got 13 percent, officials said.

Kouchner, known internationally as a founder of the medical relief group Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors without Borders), showed ignorance of the constituency in a debate with fellow candidates, admitting he did not know the names of Gardanne's districts.
Immediately after the results were known, Kouchner called on his backers to vote for the Communist candidate in the run-off "because the main goal is to halt the National Front."
Tapie won the seat in 1993 for the small left-wing Radical movement with Socialist backing with 25 percent of the vote.
The fast-talking entrepreneur hardly ever returned to his constituency and was stripped of his seat after being ruled bankrupt and convicted of fraud, tax evasion and bribery.

There were 14 candidates in the race and the abstention rate was just under 60 percent, a figure not untypical of voting trends in French by-elections which get far less media attention than general elections.
